items.stem: Which term describes a system in which rewards and positions are allocated on the basis of ability and effort rather than social background?
items.answer: Meritocracy
items.markingKey: Meritocracy: a system in which rewards and positions are allocated on the basis of ability and effort rather than social background. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “social solidarity”? Give one example.
items.answer: The sense of belonging to a society and commitment to its shared values. Example: pupils learning national history and celebrating national days.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (the sense of belonging to a society and commitment to its shared values); 1 mark for a relevant example such as pupils learning national history and celebrating national days. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “universalistic values” and “particularistic values”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Universalistic values: values and rules that apply equally to everyone, regardless of who they are (e.g. all pupils sitting the same exam marked to the same standard). Particularistic values: values and rules that apply only to a particular individual, often found in the family (e.g. parents treating a child as special because it is theirs).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: The government in Toronto expands vocational colleges to train technicians for its growing electronics industry. Suggest how a New Right sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: New Right: state education is inefficient and does not meet the needs of the economy; competition, parental choice and a market in schools will raise standards (Chubb and Moe), while education should transmit a shared national culture.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A school in Seoul begins each day with an assembly about the country’s history and its national heroes. Explain how New Right and interactionist sociologists might differ in the way they interpret this situation.
items.answer: New Right: state education is inefficient and does not meet the needs of the economy; competition, parental choice and a market in schools will raise standards (Chubb and Moe), while education should transmit a shared national culture. Interactionism: what happens inside schools matters: teachers’ labels, setting and streaming and pupils’ responses (subcultures) shape achievement through self-fulfilling prophecies (Becker, Rist, Keddie).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of participant observation for studying how far pupils in Dhaka believe that school is fair.
items.answer: Strengths: it reveals the meanings and labels that shape interaction as it happens; by joining the group the researcher can gain verstehen and see the world through members’ eyes. Limitations: it cannot measure the extent of a pattern across a whole society; it is time-consuming, costly and may put the researcher at risk. Theory: participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how far pupils in Dhaka believe that school is fair but best combined with another method such as longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Assess how useful field experiments are for studying how far pupils in Santiago believe that school is fair.
items.answer: Strengths: variables in a school, such as teacher expectations, can be altered in a normal classroom; participants usually do not know they are part of an experiment, so they act naturally. Limitations: participants have not given informed consent, which raises ethical issues; they are hard to repeat exactly because conditions in the real world change. Theory: field experiments are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how far pupils in Santiago believe that school is fair but best combined with another method such as participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Assess how useful longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) are for studying the relationship between qualifications and occupation.
items.answer: Strengths: they are ideal for tracking change in the same individuals or families over many years; they show how people’s lives change over time and allow cause and effect to be explored. Limitations: sample attrition (people dropping out) can make the sample unrepresentative over time; they are very expensive and results take many years to appear. Theory: longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce mainly quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the relationship between qualifications and occupation but best combined with another method such as covert participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “counter-school culture”, and give one example.
items.answer: A pupil subculture that rejects the values and rules of the school. Example: Willis’s “lads” who “had a laff” and rejected school work.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (a pupil subculture that rejects the values and rules of the school); 1 mark for a relevant example such as Willis’s “lads” who “had a laff” and rejected school work. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “myth of meritocracy” and “reproduction of class inequality”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Myth of meritocracy: the Marxist idea that the belief that education is fair hides how it reproduces class inequality (e.g. working-class pupils blaming themselves for low grades). Reproduction of class inequality: the process by which education passes class advantages and disadvantages from one generation to the next (e.g. middle-class children gaining the qualifications for middle-class jobs).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: In a school in Jakarta, pupils are given merit points for being on time, wearing the correct uniform and not questioning teachers. Suggest how a Marxist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Marxism: education reproduces class inequality and legitimates it: the hidden curriculum prepares working-class pupils for subordinate jobs (Bowles and Gintis), schools act as ideological state apparatuses (Althusser), and the myth of meritocracy makes failure seem the individual’s fault.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: In a school in Seoul, pupils are given merit points for being on time, wearing the correct uniform and not questioning teachers. Compare how functionalist and interactionist sociologists might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Functionalism: education performs vital functions for society: it passes on shared values and creates social solidarity (Durkheim), acts as a bridge from particularistic family values to universalistic values of wider society, and allocates people to roles on the basis of merit (Parsons, Davis and Moore). Interactionism: what happens inside schools matters: teachers’ labels, setting and streaming and pupils’ responses (subcultures) shape achievement through self-fulfilling prophecies (Becker, Rist, Keddie).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of covert participant observation for studying anti-school subcultures among working-class boys.
items.answer: Strengths: it may be the only way to study a group that hides its activities from outsiders; because the group does not know it is being studied, members act naturally and the Hawthorne effect is avoided. Limitations: studying children covertly is ethically unacceptable because they cannot consent and are vulnerable; note-taking is difficult, so data depends on memory and may be inaccurate. Theory: covert participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying anti-school subcultures among working-class boys but best combined with another method such as official statistics (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: A sociologist in Seoul wants to research anti-school subcultures among working-class boys. Evaluate the use of unstructured interviews for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: they allow people to explain the meanings they give to their experiences in their own words; rapport between interviewer and interviewee builds trust, so people may reveal more, producing valid data. Limitations: the power imbalance between adult researcher and child may make children say what they think adults want to hear; they are time-consuming and the data is hard to analyse and compare. Theory: unstructured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying anti-school subcultures among working-class boys but best combined with another method such as self-completion questionnaires (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Distinguish between “speculation” and “ideal pupil”, using an example of each.

items.stem: A sociologist in Riyadh wants to research teacher-pupil interaction in mixed-sex classrooms. Evaluate the use of self-completion questionnaires for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: they can reach a large, geographically spread sample quickly and cheaply, so findings can be generalised; they are standardised, so the study can be repeated by another researcher to check reliability. Limitations: younger respondents may misread questions or lack the concentration to complete them carefully, and may answer as they think adults expect; response rates are often low, so the sample may become unrepresentative. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying teacher-pupil interaction in mixed-sex classrooms but best combined with another method such as personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “formula funding” and “national culture”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Formula funding: funding schools according to the number of pupils they attract (e.g. a popular school receiving more money). items.stem: A sociologist in Lisbon wants to research the effects of league tables on schools. Evaluate the use of case studies for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: they can be used to generate hypotheses that are tested later on larger samples; they give a detailed, in-depth picture of one group, institution or community. Limitations: a single case cannot show how widespread a pattern is; the detailed data is difficult to compare with other cases. Theory: case studies are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce mainly qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the effects of league tables on schools but best combined with another method such as self-completion questionnaires (triangulation).

items.stem: Study the data, which come from a study of qualifications and occupation (500 adults aged 30-40, Jakarta). Table: percentage in each type of occupation | Professional/managerial job | Routine/manual job. Degree | 60% | 11%. Upper secondary only | 31% | 46%. Lower secondary or less | 17% | 74%. (a) Calculate the difference between Upper secondary only and Lower secondary or less for Professional/managerial job and for Routine/manual job, and state for which of these the difference is larger. (b) Explain one reason why these data may not give a valid picture of qualifications and occupation. (c) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that education allocates people to occupations on the basis of merit.
items.answer: (a) Professional/managerial job: 14 percentage points; Routine/manual job: 28 percentage points; the difference is larger for Routine/manual job. (b) Respondents may misunderstand questions, or give socially desirable answers, and there is no chance to clarify. (c) Evidence from the data: The figure is higher for Routine/manual job than for Professional/managerial job among Upper secondary only, Lower secondary or less; the figure is lower for Routine/manual job than for Professional/managerial job among Degree; Lower secondary or less had the highest figure for Routine/manual job. Credentialism means employers demand higher qualifications for jobs. Qualifications: The data show a link between qualifications and jobs, but not whether qualifications reflect ability or class background; Bourdieu and Bowles and Gintis argue the system favours the middle class. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 500 adults aged 30-40 in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each difference (14 and 28); 1 mark for the correct comparison. [3] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: A survey of 600 parents in Cairo produced the data below. Table: percentage of parents whose child got a place at their first-choice school | 2010 | 2025. Professional/managerial parents | 73% | 79%. Routine/manual parents | 54% | 48%. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the figure for Routine/manual parents between 2010 and 2025. Show your working. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that parental choice benefits all parents equally.
items.answer: (a) (48 − 54) ÷ 54 × 100 = -11.1%. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Professional/managerial parents; the figure fell for Routine/manual parents; Professional/managerial parents had the highest figure for 2025. Schools may “cream-skim” pupils likely to boost league table results. Qualifications: Most parents in both groups get a first choice; differences may reflect where families live; choice may still raise standards overall as the New Right claims. The data also come from official statistics of 600 parents in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for (48 − 54) ÷ 54 × 100; 1 mark for -11.1% (accept 2-3 s.f.). [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Which term describes the sense of belonging to a society and commitment to its shared values?
items.answer: Social solidarity
items.markingKey: Social solidarity: the sense of belonging to a society and commitment to its shared values. [1]

items.stem: State one criticism of the functionalist view of education.
items.answer: Education is not meritocratic: class, gender and ethnicity affect achievement.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point, e.g. education is not meritocratic: class, gender and ethnicity affect achievement. [1]

items.stem: Davis and Moore argued that education sifts and sorts people so the most able fill the most functionally important jobs. Explain this view and one criticism of it.
items.answer: Davis and Moore argued inequality is necessary to motivate the most talented to train for important roles; education is the proving ground for ability. Criticism: Tumin argued it is hard to measure functional importance and that inequality prevents talent from emerging.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Functionalism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: The government in Lisbon expands vocational colleges to train technicians for its growing electronics industry. Suggest how a New Right sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: New Right: state education is inefficient and does not meet the needs of the economy; competition, parental choice and a market in schools will raise standards (Chubb and Moe), while education should transmit a shared national culture.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A school in Dhaka begins each day with an assembly about the country’s history and its national heroes. Explain how an interactionist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Interactionism: what happens inside schools matters: teachers’ labels, setting and streaming and pupils’ responses (subcultures) shape achievement through self-fulfilling prophecies (Becker, Rist, Keddie).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: (a) Explain two functions that education performs for society according to functionalists. (b) Assess the claim that education is meritocratic.
items.answer: (a) Social solidarity and shared values (Durkheim); specialist skills; bridge between family and society (Parsons); meritocracy and role allocation (Davis and Moore); human capital. (b) For: Functionalists: equal opportunities, universalistic standards, achieved status (Parsons); role allocation (Davis and Moore); expansion of education and rising attainment. Against: Marxists: myth of meritocracy (Bowles and Gintis); class, gender and ethnic gaps; cultural capital (Bourdieu); private schooling; labelling (Becker); social mobility remains limited. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement on how far the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Level 1 (1-3): one or two simple points, limited sociological knowledge. Level 2 (4-6): explained points using some concepts, studies or theories. Level 3 (7-8): two well-explained, developed points with accurate concepts, studies or theories, clearly applied to the question. Creditworthy: Social solidarity and shared values (Durkheim); specialist skills; bridge between family and society (Parsons); meritocracy and role allocation (Davis and Moore); human capital. [8] (b) Level 1 (1-3): a few simple points. Level 2 (4-6): some explained arguments, mainly on one side; limited evaluation. Level 3 (7-9): a range of explained arguments and evidence for and against, with some evaluation. Level 4 (10-12): a balanced, well-supported analysis using theories, studies and concepts, sustained evaluation and a reasoned conclusion. For: Functionalists: equal opportunities, universalistic standards, achieved status (Parsons); role allocation (Davis and Moore); expansion of education and rising attainment. Against: Marxists: myth of meritocracy (Bowles and Gintis); class, gender and ethnic gaps; cultural capital (Bourdieu); private schooling; labelling (Becker); social mobility remains limited. [12]

items.stem: Which term describes the process by which education passes class advantages and disadvantages from one generation to the next?
items.answer: Reproduction of class inequality
items.markingKey: Reproduction of class inequality: the process by which education passes class advantages and disadvantages from one generation to the next. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Bowles and Gintis argued that schools reward creativity and independence.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. They found schools rewarded conformity and obedience, and penalised creativity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the correct judgement; 1 mark for an accurate sociological explanation. [2]

items.stem: A group of working-class boys in Riyadh mock pupils who work hard, skip lessons and say they will “get a job in the factory anyway”. Suggest how a liberal feminist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Liberal feminism: education has helped reduce gender inequality through equal opportunities policies, but stereotyping, subject choice and the hidden curriculum still steer girls and boys in different directions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Study the following extract (Source A) from a report on research carried out in Mumbai. “A researcher observed lessons in four secondary schools in Madrid over a term. Pupils who sat quietly, followed instructions and handed work in on time received the highest grades for “effort”, even when their work was less original than that of pupils who questioned the teacher.” (a) Identify the main research method used in the study described in Source A. (b) Explain how a Marxist sociologist might interpret the findings in Source A.
items.answer: (a) Non-participant observation. (b) The findings support the correspondence principle: schools reward obedience and conformity, preparing pupils to be compliant workers (Bowles and Gintis).
items.markingKey: (a) Non-participant observation. [1] (b) 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the findings in the source. [3]

items.stem: A group of working-class boys in Mumbai mock pupils who work hard, skip lessons and say they will “get a job in the factory anyway”. Explain how a liberal feminist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Liberal feminism: education has helped reduce gender inequality through equal opportunities policies, but stereotyping, subject choice and the hidden curriculum still steer girls and boys in different directions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using semi-structured interviews to research anti-school subcultures among working-class boys.
items.answer: Strengths: open follow-up questions let interviewees explain their reasoning; they are more flexible than structured interviews but easier to analyse than unstructured ones. Limitations: follow-up questions differ between interviews, so reliability is lower than with a fixed schedule; samples are usually fairly small, so representativeness is limited. Theory: semi-structured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative and quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying anti-school subcultures among working-class boys but best combined with another method such as longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]

items.stem: Which term describes the unofficial messages about gender roles conveyed through school organisation, teacher attention and resources?
items.answer: Hidden curriculum (gender)
items.markingKey: Hidden curriculum (gender): the unofficial messages about gender roles conveyed through school organisation, teacher attention and resources. [1]

items.stem: Explain two ways in which feminists argue education reinforces gender inequality.
items.answer: Gendered subject choice and careers advice; hidden curriculum of teacher attention and stereotyping (Spender); patriarchal curriculum marginalising women; sexual harassment and policing of girls’ behaviour; male-dominated leadership.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each explained way. [4]

items.stem: A sociologist in Cairo wants to research how pupils respond to teachers’ labels. Explain one strength of using participant observation for this research.
items.answer: It reveals the meanings and labels that shape interaction as it happens.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant strength; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of how pupils respond to teachers’ labels. [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using field experiments to research how pupils respond to teachers’ labels.
items.answer: Strengths: variables in a school, such as teacher expectations, can be altered in a normal classroom; one variable can be altered (for example the name on a job application) to test its effect. Limitations: deceiving people about sensitive matters may cause harm or distress; they are hard to repeat exactly because conditions in the real world change. Theory: field experiments are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how pupils respond to teachers’ labels but best combined with another method such as personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: State one policy associated with the marketisation of education.
items.answer: Formula funding based on pupil numbers.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point, e.g. formula funding based on pupil numbers. [1]

items.stem: Explain two features of the New Right view of education.
items.answer: State education is inefficient and unresponsive; competition and parental choice raise standards; schools should be run like businesses; education should serve the economy; it should transmit a shared national culture.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each explained feature. [4]

items.stem: The government in Santiago publishes school league tables and allows parents to apply to any school; popular schools fill up quickly with pupils from nearby wealthy areas. Suggest how a neoliberal sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Neoliberalism: education should be run as a market: schools compete for pupils, parents act as consumers and the state’s role is minimal; this raises efficiency and standards.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of participant observation for studying how parents choose secondary schools in Colombo.
items.answer: Strengths: it reveals the meanings and labels that shape interaction as it happens; the researcher sees what people actually do in their natural setting, not just what they say, so validity is high. Limitations: it cannot measure the extent of a pattern across a whole society; the observer’s presence may change the group’s behaviour (the Hawthorne effect), especially if overt. Theory: participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how parents choose secondary schools in Colombo but best combined with another method such as official statistics (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]
